description: We are building an AgTech decision-support tool for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data). Led by an Agricultural Biotechnologist handling the core plant physiology, crop stress parameters,and NASA dataset logic (SMAP, ECOSTRESS, GPM), we are seeking motivated technical collaborators in software engineering, data science, and UI/UX design to help process spatial feeds, build our web dashboard, and shape our final submission.
summary: A healthy-looking crop and a high yield does not necessarily guarantee nutritionally adequate food. ZINCWISE explores this overlooked gap in agriculture by connecting climate and soil conditions with crop-nutrition research, helping farmers look beyond yield towards the nutritional potential of their harvest. ZINCWISE is an interactive, farmer-focused decision-support platform designed for Punjab, Pakistan, initially focusing on wheat and zinc nutrition. It integrates NASA Earth observation datasets (SMAP, GPM IMERG, GLDAS and MERRA-2) with research-based wheat rotation options suited to regional conditions. Farmers can enter their location to explore regionally suitable wheat-based crop-rotation options and explore potential environmental constraints. Those with soil-test results can enter additional information, such as pH and organic matter, to receive more detailed insights into conditions that may affect zinc availability and crop nutrition. By combining Earth observation data with agricultural and nutritional research, ZINCWISE aims to support more informed farming decisions that consider not only how much food is produced, but also its nutritional quality.
details:
ZINCWISE: Beyond Yield — Mapping the Nutritional Blind Spots in Agriculture.

A successful wheat harvest does not necessarily mean nutritionally adequate grain. Yield measures how much food is produced, but not how much zinc reaches the edible grain. This distinction is particularly important in Punjab, Pakistan, where wheat is a major dietary staple and an important source of zinc. Zinc must be available in the soil, absorbed by plant roots and transported to the developing grain. Yet these processes are not captured by yield figures alone.

ZINCWISE is a farmer-focused decision-support platform that brings environmental conditions, soil-test information and agricultural research together to explore factors influencing zinc availability in wheat cultivation. It works through two independent levels of assessment.

At the first level, farmers enter their location to explore environmental conditions relevant to wheat cultivation, including rainfall, temperature and soil-moisture patterns over relevant growing periods. ZINCWISE integrates NASA Earth observation datasets, including SMAP, GPM IMERG, GLDAS and MERRA-2, to provide this environmental context. It then provides potential wheat-based crop rotations, such as wheat–mungbean and wheat–chickpea, identified through published agricultural research.

At the second level, farmers can enter results from their own laboratory soil tests, including pH, organic matter, soil texture and, where available, laboratory-measured extractable zinc. These results allow the platform to provide more deeper insights into soil conditions associated with zinc availability.

What makes ZINCWISE distinctive is its focus on the nutritional blind spot between agricultural productivity and food quality. Rather than treating a good harvest as the only measure of success, it brings attention to the environmental and soil factors that may influence the movement of zinc from soil into crops. It also combines two different sources of information: large-scale satellite observations and field-specific soil-test results.

The platform explores wheat-based rotations through published evidence on soil fertility, nutrient cycling, water requirements and agronomic suitability. These options are presented as potential agricultural strategies, not guaranteed methods of increasing grain zinc. Similarly, NASA observations provide environmental context; they do not directly measure soil or grain zinc. ZINCWISE does not claim to predict grain zinc concentrations, which require appropriate laboratory testing.

By making environmental information and agricultural research more accessible, ZINCWISE aims to help farmers make more informed crop-rotation decisions and recognise potential soil-related nutritional constraints. Its broader intended impact is to encourage agricultural planning that considers not only how much food is produced, but also the conditions that influence its nutritional potential.

Scientific accuracy and data limitations guided the development of ZINCWISE. NASA datasets provide environmental context, not direct measurements of soil or grain zinc; their spatial and temporal resolutions also differ. Soil-test interpretations account for the laboratory extraction method when extractable zinc is provided, while other soil properties offer supporting context rather than proof of zinc deficiency. Crop rotations are presented as research-supported options, not guaranteed ways to increase grain zinc. Actual grain zinc concentration requires laboratory analysis.

Tools, Languages and Software Used
  • Front-end and visualisation: Next.js, React, TypeScript, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and Leaflet.
  • Data processing and remote sensing: Python, and Google Earth Engine.
